one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban writes the fourth installment of his biographical-naming series, triggered by Mohagher Iqbal -- chief peace negotiator of the Moro Islamic Liberation Front -- using an alias or nom de guerre that has disrupted the peace process unnecessarily in CJP's humble view. Despite being pressed to reveal his real name, Iqbal has remained tightlipped, claiming pseudonyms are normal for revolutionaries; in a GMA News TV 'Balitanghali' interview he said: 'Kahit na si Marcelo del Pilar siyam po ang pangalan, at maging ang tatay ni Presidente na si Ninoy Aquino, in his passport his name was Marcial Bonifacio. So, normal po yan.' Under Republic Act No. 6085, which regulates alias use, no person shall use any name different from (1) the one registered at birth in the local civil registry, (2) baptized for the first time, (3) for an alien -- registered in the bureau of immigration upon entry, or (4) such substitute name as may have been authorized by a competent court -- with exceptions for literary, cinema, TV, radio or other entertainment purposes and in athletic events (Heart Evangelista; Pacman; Pancho Villa). The Civil Code allows a married woman three naming options: (1) maiden first name and surname plus husband's surname, (2) maiden first name plus husband's surname, or (3) husband's full name prefixed with 'Mrs.' -- CJP applies this to his wife: (1) Elenita Carpio Panganiban, (2) Elenita Panganiban, or (3) Mrs. Artemio V. Panganiban. The Civil Code also permits pen names or stage names in good faith without injury to third persons, making 'Doveglion' (Jose Garcia Villa) and 'Quijano de Manila' (Nick Joaquin) perfectly legal. Filipino nicknames -- not expressly allowed by RA 6085 or the Civil Code -- have acquired legal acquiescence: P-Noy, GMA, Erap, FVR, Cory, FM are used without nitpicking. Special laws expressly bar aliases: BSP Circular 251 forbids 'Jose Pidal' or 'Jose Velarde' in bank accounts; fictitious names are not authorized on passports, driver's licenses, and other government-issued IDs precisely because they identify holders. RA 6085 penalizes illegal aliases with imprisonment from 1 to 5 years and a fine of P5,000 to P10,000. Despite these penalties, revolutionaries still use noms de guerre to confuse enemies, avoid capture, and spare their families inconvenience and possible ridicule. Spies and deep-penetration agents like the legendary James Bond employ many names and passports -- stealth and subterfuge are essential to their work -- but this does not make the practice legal; rebels face graver risks of prosecution for rebellion, sedition or murder, so alias prosecution is the least of their worries. Meanwhile, Iqbal and his associates are in no danger of arrest because they have been issued 'safe conduct' passes; should the peace process collapse, the passes would expire; should it succeed, they could be hailed as heroes. Despite the illegal use of a nom de guerre, Iqbal's acts cannot be deemed invalid or illegal -- they were done with the authority of the MILF, whose leadership has expressly affirmed his authority and the binding effect of his acts. Moreover, the government peace panel headed by Miriam Coronel Ferrer (including Sec Teresita Deles) admitted knowledge of Iqbal's nom de guerre and his real name. Once the Bangsamoro Basic Law is approved, it would bind the Republic regardless of the validity of the Comprehensive Agreement on the Bangsamoro he signed -- assuming it passes judicial scrutiny, the BBL would become part of the law of the land. What's in a name? To many of us, it is our most cherished treasure because it bears our honor and worth as distinct human beings -- especially for members of the judiciary. SC justices always sign their decisions with their complete names including middle initials, as in Maria Lourdes P.A. Sereno or Hilario G. Davide Jr. One way of incurring their ire is to misspell their names or to muddle their middle initials.
